{{Short description|Model of molecular evolution}}
The '''Infinite sites model''' (ISM) is a mathematical model of [[molecular evolution]] first proposed by [[Motoo Kimura]] in 1969.<ref name=":2" /> Like other mutation models, the ISM provides a basis for understanding how mutation develops new alleles in DNA sequences. Using allele frequencies, it allows for the calculation of [[heterozygosity]], or [[genetic diversity]], in a finite population and for the estimation of [[genetic distance]]s between populations of interest.

The assumptions of the ISM are that (1) there are an infinite number of sites where mutations can occur, (2) every new mutation occurs at a novel site, and (3) there is no [[Genetic recombination|recombination]].<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":0">{{cite journal | last1 = Tajima | first1 = F | year = 1996 | title = Infinite-allele model and infinite-site model in population genetics | journal = Journal of Genetics | volume = 75 | pages = 27–31 | doi=10.1007/bf02931749| s2cid = 1330336 }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{cite journal | last1 = Watterson | first1 = GA | year = 1975 | title = On the number of segregating sites in genetical models without recombination | journal = Theoretical Population Biology | volume = 7 | issue = 2| pages = 256–276 | doi=10.1016/0040-5809(75)90020-9 | pmid=1145509| bibcode = 1975TPBio...7..256W }}</ref> The term ‘site’ refers to a single nucleotide base pair.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|title = The Number of Heterozygous Nucleotide Sites Maintained in a Finite Population Due to Steady Flux of Mutations|journal = Genetics|date = 1969-04-01|issn = 0016-6731|pmc = 1212250|pmid = 5364968|pages = 893–903|volume = 61|issue = 4|first = Motoo|last = Kimura|doi = 10.1093/genetics/61.4.893}}</ref> Because every new mutation has to occur at a novel site, there can be no [[homoplasy]], or back-mutation to an allele that previously existed. All identical alleles are [[identical by descent]]. The [[Four-gamete test|four gamete rule]] can be applied to the data to ensure that they do not violate the model assumption of no recombination.<ref>{{Cite journal

The mutation rate (<math>\theta</math>) can be estimated as follows, where <math>\mu^*</math> is the number of mutations found within a randomly selected DNA sequence (per generation) and <math>N_e</math> is the [[effective population size]].<ref name=":3">{{cite journal | last1 = Futschik | first1 = A | last2 = Gach | first2 = F | year = 2008 | title = On the inadmissibility of Watterson's estimator | journal = Theoretical Population Biology | volume = 73 | issue = 2| pages = 212–221 | doi=10.1016/j.tpb.2007.11.009| pmid = 18215409 | bibcode = 2008TPBio..73..212F }}</ref> The [[coefficient]] is the product of twice the gene copies in individuals of the population; in the case of diploid, biparentally-inherited genes, the appropriate coefficient is 4, whereas for uniparental, haploid genes, such as mitochondrial genes, the coefficient would be 2 but applied to the ''female'' effective population size which is, for most species, roughly half of <math>N_e</math>.

<math>\theta=4N_e\mu^*

</math>

When considering the length of a DNA sequence, the expected number of mutations is calculated as:

<math>\mu^*=k\mu</math>

where k is the length of a DNA sequence and <math>\mu</math> is the probability a mutation will occur at a site.<ref name=":3" />

Watterson developed an estimator for mutation rate that incorporates the number of segregating sites [[Watterson estimator|(Watterson's estimator)]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Ramirez-Soriano | first1 = A | last2 = Nielsen | first2 = R | year = 2009 | title = Correcting Estimators of Θ and Tajima's D for Ascertainment Biases Caused by the Single-Nucleotide Polymorphism Discovery Process | journal = Genetics | volume = 181 | issue = 2| pages = 701–710 | doi=10.1534/genetics.108.094060| pmid = 19087964 | pmc = 2644958 }}</ref>

One way to think of the ISM is in how it applies to genome evolution. To understand the ISM as it applies to genome evolution, we must think of this model as it applies to [[chromosome]]s. Chromosomes are made up of ''sites'', which are [[nucleotide]]s represented by either A, C, G, or T. While individual chromosomes are not infinite, we must think of chromosomes as continuous intervals or continuous circles.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last1=Ma|first1=Jian|last2=Ratan|first2=Aakrosh|last3=Raney|first3=Brian J.|last4=Suh|first4=Bernard B.|last5=Miller|first5=Webb|last6=Haussler|first6=David|date=2008-09-23|title=The infinite sites model of genome evolution|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=105|issue=38|pages=14254–14261|doi=10.1073/pnas.0805217105|issn=0027-8424|pmc=2533685|pmid=18787111|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Multiple assumptions are applied to understanding the ISM in terms of genome evolution:<ref name=":4" />
* ''k'' breaks are made in these chromosomes, which leaves ''2k'' free ends available. The ''2k'' free ends will rejoin in a new manner rearranging the set of chromosomes (i.e. [[Chromosomal translocation|reciprocal translocation]], [[Fusion gene|fusion, fission]], [[Chromosomal inversion|inversion]], circularized incision, circularized excision).
* No break point is ever used twice.
* A set of chromosomes can be duplicated or lost.
* DNA that never existed before can be observed in the chromosomes, such as [[horizontal gene transfer]] of DNA or viral integration.
* If the chromosomes become different enough, evolution can form a new species.
* Substitutions that alter a single base pair are individually invisible and substitutions occur at a finite rate per site.
* The substitution rate is the same for all sites in a species, but is allowed to vary between species (i.e. no [[molecular clock]] is assumed).
* Instead of thinking about substitutions themselves, think about the effect of the substitution at each point along the chromosome as a continuous increase in evolutionary distance between the previous version of the genome at that site and the next version of the genome at the corresponding site in the descendant.<ref name=":4" />
